draft.title: Extended metaphor
card: A metaphor says one thing is another, such as "Time is a thief." It compares two things without using like or as.
An extended metaphor keeps the same comparison going through several lines, a stanza or a whole text. Each new line adds another detail to the comparison.
Example: a writer calls life a journey, then adds a crossroads, a rough road and a map. Roads, crossroads and maps all belong to the journey comparison.
The effect is to build one clear picture in the reader's mind. It lets the writer explore an idea in more depth than a single metaphor can.
draft.remember: An extended metaphor keeps one comparison going and adds new details to it.

a.q: Which of these is an extended metaphor?
opts: My mind was a garden: thoughts sprouted and doubts were weeds
My mind was a garden, and I was tired after the long test
My mind was like a garden where thoughts grew in the sun
My mind raced, my hands shook and my heart pounded
a.why: The first option keeps the garden comparison going with sprouting thoughts and weeds. The third option also compares a mind to a garden, but it uses like, so it is a simile, and it adds no further details.
a.clue: Look for one comparison that keeps adding new parts.

b.q: Jess writes that the school year was a long voyage, term one was the launch, exams were storms and holidays were safe harbours. What does this show?
opts: An extended metaphor that treats the year as a sea voyage
A single metaphor that compares the year to one storm
A simile that uses like or as to compare a year and a ship
A list of facts about the school year and sea travel
b.why: The year is compared to a voyage, and the launch, storms and harbours each add a detail to that one comparison, so it is extended. A single metaphor would stop after the first comparison. There is no like or as, so it is not a simile.
b.clue: Count how many parts of the voyage comparison appear.
